newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit gathers to clear single currency hurdles.
newsitem.headline: EU summit gathers to clear single currency hurdles.

text.p: European Union leaders gathered on Friday to clear key hurdles to a single European currency in 1999 after finance ministers came close to agreement on a budget discipline pact in 11-hour marathon talks.

The 15 leaders were to debate the path to economic and monetary union at the first session of their two-day summit in the Irish capital after finance ministers worked until 3 a.m. (0300 GMT) to draft proposals for a pact on fiscal discipline.
"The accord has been virtually reached. We are satisfied that great progress has been made," Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters.
Later on Friday, the European Monetary Institute is due to unveil symbolically the first euro banknotes, which will enter the pockets of hundreds of millions of Europeans from 2002.

But EU heads of state and government must first resolve the remaining details on the stability pact, intended to ensure that countries which join the single currency respect tight budget deficit limits thereafter.
Germany, whose citizens are wary of giving up the hard deutschemark for the untried euro, has pressed for watertight hefty sanctions on any country that overspends.

Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, who chaired the overnight talks, made clear the summit still had to endorse a compromise proposal which fell well short of Bonn's original demands for automatic fines on budget sinners.

The compromise on the key issue of exceptional circumstances that would justify breaching the deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product would leave a final political judgment to the EU's council of ministers -- a key French demand.
"We have an agreement on the architecture of the stability pact," a confident French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said. "There is nothing left which is of a nature to prevent an agreement."
An Irish official said the final political decision to accept the compromise rested with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Financial markets, which opened steady, seemed satisfied with the compromise but were looking for a quick endorsement from the EU leaders.

The European Commission launched a publicity campaign to ease public acceptance of the new currency earlier this week, unveiling a dollar-style symbol -- a "c" with two horizantal dashes through it -- which it is to represent the euro.

The growing sense of inevitability about monetary union could make this an uncomfortable summit for British Prime Minister John Major, whose Conservative government, deeply torn over European policy, lost its parliamentary majority on Thursday when the opposition Labour party won a by-election.
Major, facing an election by May, is under strong pressure from Eurosceptics in his party to end his wait-and-see approach to monetary union and rule out joining the single currency.

The British leader will also be seeking to resist any move towards closer European integration on the summit's other main agenda item -- a drive to reform EU institutions in preparation for admitting former communist central European countries from around the year 2000.

The Irish presidency of the EU has produced a report to increase cooperation in foreign, defence, interior and justice affairs but it has left aside for now the issue of greater majority voting most sensitive to Britain.
"I don't think it's going to be a summit in which serious decisions are going to be taken," Major told reporters.

France and Germany put forward their own proposals for greater integration on Monday, saying it was vital to give the slow-moving negotiations new momentum if a substantial reform is to be achieve by the deadline of next June in Amsterdam.
